Produce and alliums keep a very long time if you can try to mimic a cellar as much as possible -- dry, cool, dark. If not just leave them on the counter and make sure they stay dry, you'll still wind up using them I'm sure. I keep a mix of both dry and canned beans on hand, canned tomatoes, dry pasta, canned fish, frozen peas. 

Really though you need to just plan your meals better. Go to the store once a week and only buy stuff you are going to cook. Going more than once is ideal if you have the time or don't want to eat leftovers all week. A lot of fresh produce can still last a long time. Root vegetables you can throw in the fridge in a tupperware full of water and they stay crisp for weeks instead of going limp after 2 days. Oh, cabbage seems to last forever. Squash does too. 

Really though unless you want to eat frozen foods you need to go at least once a week. Learn to enjoy it, take inspiration from the seasonal produce in deciding what to cook. Let a pretty veg or cut of meat dictate your meals.

Moving to a major metropolitan area. I'm guilty of it as well, I moved to the Pacific Northwest because I was sick of living in the southern region. I do wonder what life would have been like here 20 years ago when you could afford to live relatively cheaply, travel around without much traffic, actually do the beautiful hikes without 100 other people. One time I wanted to do a very popular hike, got there at 8am and saw probably 200 cars. Gave up and took a day off work during the week and hit it at 7am, saw a whopping 4 cars then. Sure I can do non-social media view hikes that are fantastic still, but sometimes I do want that awe-inducing overlook. Just think of all that kind of stuff our parents and grandparents got to enjoy that we don't. The monetary quality of life they had from a single job is of course the main thing, but being able to drive without massive traffic, random camping along a lake that's not all bought up cabins now, etc. I'd love that.

If your oven has a light inside that's an easy way to do it, just make sure you don't accidentally bake your starter. I personally throw mine ontop of my water heater.

I never follow strict guidelines. Probably do about 3/4cup flour and half a cup water. I like mine pretty loose so it's easier to mix in the container I use. I never throw starter out either, sometimes I'll have almost a pint built up before I make some stuff (either dough or use the starter for pancakes just to get rid of some). They're pretty indestructible too. I keep mine in the fridge and feed every few weeks if I'm not using it. I once went 4mo and figured it was dead. No mold or anything on it and after a single feeding it was doubling again.
